what: A search index like Elasticsearch or OpenSearch finds documents by the words inside them, ranks them by relevance, and answers in milliseconds - even across billions of documents.
like: Like the index at the back of a book: look up a word and it lists every page that word appears on.
why: Fast full-text search with typo-tolerant, ranked results that SQL LIKE cannot match
Filters, facets (counts per category) and aggregations on the same query
Scales out by splitting data into shards, and keeps replica copies for safety and read speed

nodes.t: Primary shards|data split by doc id

steps.d: An analyzer runs on every text field: a tokenizer splits it into words, then filters lowercase them and stem them (foxes becomes fox). The same analyzer runs on the query, so both match.
The inverted index is a sorted list of every unique term, each with the list of documents that contain it. Searching means looking up a few terms, not scanning every document.
An index is split into primary shards, each a small search engine (a Lucene index). The primary count is set when you create the index; replicas copy each shard to other nodes.
A coordinator node sends the query to one copy of every shard, each returns its best hits, and the coordinator merges them into one ranked page of results.
BM25 scores a match higher when the term is rare across all documents, appears often in this one (with diminishing returns), and the field is short.
New documents land in a buffer. A refresh, every 1 second by default on recently searched indices, writes them as a new segment so searches can see them - near real time.

numbers.l: default refresh interval before new documents become searchable
keep documents per shard below this
BM25 defaults: k1 (term saturation) and b (length normalisation)
default rank constant when RRF merges keyword and vector results

choices.d: Decide per field: text (analyzed, for full-text search) or keyword (exact value, for filters, sorting and facets). Pick a language analyzer so stemming fits your users.
Primaries are fixed at index creation (default 1), so size for growth at 10-50 GB per shard. Replicas (default 1) can change any time and add read capacity and safety.
1 s gives near real-time search. For big bulk loads set it longer, or -1 to switch it off, then turn it back on - indexing gets much faster.
Point the app at an alias, not an index. Build a new index with the new mapping, reindex into it, then swap the alias in one atomic step - no downtime.
BM25 for exact words, names and codes; vector (kNN) search for meaning; hybrid runs both and merges the lists with RRF or score normalisation.

instead.why: Small data: Postgres full-text search avoids running a second system
Pure meaning-based search over embeddings, no keyword ranking needed
Keyword plus vector retrieval feeding an LLM in a RAG pipeline
Heavy SQL analytics and joins over history, not text search

breaks.d: The sync job lags or drops events, so search shows old prices or deleted items.
breaks.see: CDC consumer lag rising; users find items that no longer exist
breaks.fix: Stream changes with CDC, make updates idempotent by id, and run a regular full reindex to catch drift

breaks.d: Too many tiny shards waste memory; too few huge ones are slow to search and recover.
breaks.see: High heap use with many small shards, or shards far over 50 GB
breaks.fix: Aim for 10-50 GB per shard; split or reindex behind an alias

breaks.d: A field's type or analyzer cannot change on an existing index.
breaks.see: Mapping errors, or a field that will not filter or sort
breaks.fix: Create a new index, reindex, then swap the alias

breaks.d: Refreshing every second while loading millions of documents creates many small segments.
breaks.see: Low indexing rate and lots of merge activity
breaks.fix: Raise the refresh interval or set it to -1 during the load, use the bulk API, add replicas after

breaks.d: Asking for page 5,000 makes every shard sort and return thousands of hits; from + size is capped at 10,000 by default.
breaks.see: Slow, memory-heavy queries, or result window errors past 10,000
breaks.fix: Page with search_after and a sort key instead of a large from

say: The database stays the source of truth, and Elasticsearch is a read-optimised copy built for search.
Changes flow from the database through CDC into a queue, and an indexer upserts documents by id, so replays are safe.
Search is near real time - new data shows up within about a second after a refresh - and the product is fine with that.
The app talks to an alias, so when the mapping changes I build a new index, reindex, and swap the alias with no downtime.

followups.q: Why not just use SQL LIKE '%term%'?
followups.a: A leading wildcard cannot use a normal B-tree index, so the database scans every row. It also cannot stem words, handle typos or rank by relevance. An inverted index looks up terms directly and scores results with BM25.

followups.q: How do you keep search in sync with the database?
followups.a: Capture row changes with CDC (reading the database log), send them through a queue, and upsert by document id. Updates are idempotent, so retries are safe. A scheduled full reindex catches anything missed.

followups.q: Can I use Elasticsearch as my main database?
followups.a: Better not. It is built for search, not transactions, and new writes only become searchable after a refresh. Keep a real database as the source of truth so you can always rebuild the index.

followups.q: How would you add semantic search?
followups.a: Store an embedding per document in a dense vector field and run kNN search. For best results run hybrid: BM25 and kNN together, merged with reciprocal rank fusion, then optionally a reranker on the top hits.

today: Elasticsearch 9.0 (April 2025) made BBQ - Better Binary Quantization, a way to shrink vectors so vector search uses far less memory - generally available, and OpenSearch has offered built-in hybrid search since 2.10.

check.q: What does an inverted index map?
check.a: Each term to the list of documents that contain it
d: Each document to its row on disk
Each user to their recent searches
check.why: Looking up a term gives its matching documents straight away, which is why full-text search is fast.

check.q: You index a document and search for it straight away, but it is not found. Why?
check.a: It becomes visible after the next refresh, about 1 second
d: The replica must be rebuilt first
Documents are searchable only after a nightly job
check.why: Search is near real time: a refresh turns new documents into a searchable segment.

check.q: You need to change a field's analyzer in production. What is the safe way?
check.a: New index, reindex, then swap the alias
d: Restart the cluster with the new setting
check.why: Existing fields keep their mapping, so you rebuild and switch atomically behind an alias.

check.q: In BM25, which match tends to score highest?
check.a: A rare term in a short field
d: A common word like 'the' in a long field
Any term in the newest document
A term in the largest document
check.why: Rare terms carry more meaning, and short fields are not diluted by extra words.
